opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most fundamental questions we can ask, and my view is that interaction with other agents isn't just a nice-to-have for intelligence, it's plausibly one of the main drivers of it.

Consider what a single agent faces in a static environment. Once you've solved the task, there's no pressure to get any smarter. The environment doesn't fight back, it doesn't adapt to you, and it doesn't present new problems unless you hand-design them. As soon as you have other learning agents in the world, the environment becomes non-stationary. Whatever you learn changes what the others should do, which changes what you should do, and so on. That gives you an automatic curriculum, an open-ended source of novelty, without anyone having to engineer it.

There's an evolutionary argument too, sometimes called the social intelligence hypothesis. The hardest thing in a primate's environment probably wasn't finding fruit or avoiding predators. It was dealing with other primates: figuring out who's an ally, who's deceiving you, how to coordinate, how to build reputation. Those problems are recursive. To predict my behavior you need to model me, and I need to model you modeling me. That kind of theory-of-mind reasoning seems to require exactly the abstract, flexible cognition we associate with intelligence.

Then there's communication, which is very close to my own research. Language exists because there are other agents to talk to. Once you have a shared communication channel, you can transmit knowledge across individuals and across generations, and that's what makes cultural accumulation possible. Humans individually aren't that impressive, but we're incredibly good at learning from each other and building on what came before. A lot of what we call human intelligence is really collective, distributed across people, institutions, and artifacts.

What interests me from a machine learning perspective is that we still don't know how to fully harness this. Self-play gave us superhuman Go and poker, but those are two-player zero-sum games, where things are relatively well-behaved. The real world is general-sum: mixed cooperation and competition. There, naive independent learning often fails. Agents end up in poor equilibria, or learn conventions that only work with the specific partners they trained with. That's why we've worked on things like opponent-shaping methods such as LOLA, where agents account for the fact that others are learning too, and zero-shot coordination, where you want agents that can coordinate with novel partners, including humans, without having agreed on arbitrary conventions in advance.

So my short answer: other agents create the open-ended, adaptive, recursive problems that demand intelligence, and they also provide the channel, communication and culture, through which intelligence compounds. If we want artificial systems that are generally intelligent and that work well alongside people, I think multi-agent learning has to be central to that story rather than an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction among agents drives intelligence and describes adaptive, recursive challenges and shared culture as ways intelligence develops and compounds.

r002.rationale: It says the hardest part of primates’ environment was dealing with other primates, whose social challenges demand flexible cognition associated with intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is something I think about a lot, and I'd frame it like this: if you look at where intelligence came from in the natural world, it didn't come from a single agent solving a fixed optimisation problem. It came from populations of agents interacting with each other, over and over, where the environment that any one agent faces is largely made up of other agents who are themselves learning and adapting. That's a fundamentally different kind of problem from, say, image classification, where the data distribution is stationary and you're just trying to fit it.

The key property is that multi-agent settings are non-stationary from the point of view of each individual. Whatever I learn to do, you can learn to respond to, and so the thing I was optimising against has moved. That creates a kind of open-ended curriculum. Nobody has to hand-design increasingly hard tasks, because the other agents are doing it for you. We saw a very clean version of this with self-play in games like Go, and in things like hide-and-seek environments where agents invent tool use and counter-strategies that the designers never specified. The complexity of behaviour emerges from the interaction, not from the reward function.

And then I think there's a second, more subtle piece, which is that a lot of what we call intelligence in humans is really social cognition. Theory of mind, language, conventions, norms, the ability to coordinate with strangers on an ad hoc basis. None of that makes any sense for a solitary agent. Language in particular only exists because there's someone to communicate with, and it only gets shaped into something useful through the pressure of needing to be understood. So in my group we spend a lot of time on cooperative multi-agent problems, things like Hanabi or zero-shot coordination, precisely because that's where you have to reason about what another agent believes, what they can infer from your actions, and how to make yourself interpretable. I'd argue those capabilities are closer to the core of general intelligence than beating a human at chess.

The flip side, and I want to be honest about this, is that multi-agent learning is also hard and fragile. Self-play can collapse into weird conventions that only work with copies of yourself. Agents can get stuck in equilibria that are stable but bad. So you can't just throw a bunch of learners in a room and expect intelligence to fall out. The research question for me is really: what are the right inductive biases, the right structure on the problem, such that the interaction pressure pushes towards robust, general, human-compatible behaviour rather than towards brittle idiosyncrasies? That's the interesting frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence arose from populations of agents interacting and that complex behavior emerges from those interactions.

r002.rationale: It says an agent’s environment is largely made up of other learning agents and links interaction to human social cognition, but does not identify other agents as the environment’s most complex parts.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the key ideas is that other agents make the learning problem continually change. If you’re trying to solve a fixed task, you can eventually find a strategy that works and stop improving. But if you’re interacting with another learner, then as you get better, they adapt, and that creates new challenges for you. So you have this potential for an open-ended process where increasingly sophisticated behaviour becomes useful.

Competition is one example, but cooperation is just as interesting. If we need to achieve something together, I have to work out what you’re going to do, what you know, and perhaps what you think I know. Communication becomes valuable because it lets us coordinate. Those pressures can give rise to capabilities that wouldn’t be particularly useful for an agent acting alone.

And there’s a subtle distinction here: I’m not just acting in an environment that happens to contain you. My behaviour can change your behaviour—and even change what you learn. Once you take that seriously, reasoning about the interaction itself becomes part of the problem.

That doesn’t mean putting a bunch of agents together automatically produces intelligence. The incentives, the tasks, and the learning dynamics matter enormously. But multi-agent interaction gives us a mechanism for generating new learning challenges, rather than having to specify every challenge ourselves.

r001.rationale: It describes increasingly sophisticated behavior emerging through interactions that continually change the learning challenges.

r002.rationale: It says other agents shape learning challenges and capabilities, but does not identify them as the most complex parts of environments shaping human cognitive capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interaction with other agents gives you a very natural curriculum. As the agents around you become more capable, the problems you have to solve become harder. You can’t just learn a fixed solution and be done, because the thing you’re interacting with is also learning and adapting.

And that creates a need for quite sophisticated reasoning. What does the other agent know? What are they trying to achieve? How will they respond to what I do? In cooperative settings, you also have to figure out how to communicate and coordinate, potentially with someone you haven’t encountered before.

But I wouldn’t say that putting a bunch of agents together automatically produces intelligence. They can also settle into very simple behaviours. The interesting question is what kinds of environments and incentives make increasingly sophisticated strategies useful, and whether those strategies generalise beyond the particular agents you trained with.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction creates a curriculum and motivates sophisticated reasoning, but does not clearly present intelligence itself as emerging from interactions among agents. It also cautions that putting agents together does not automatically produce intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response describes other agents as learning and adapting, but does not identify them as the most complex parts of the environments shaping human cognitive capabilities.
